title: A 10-Minute X-Ray Flash May Mark the Birth of a Magnetar
summary:
Astronomers have long identified collisions between neutron stars by brief bursts of gamma rays, which can vanish in less than two seconds. Now, new research suggests that some mergers may also produce X-ray flashes that stay visible for several minutes. One event, detected on July 4, 2025, by the SVOM, Insight-HXMT and Einstein Probe satellites, showed exactly that. Its gamma-ray burst lasted only about half a second, but the Einstein Probe recorded bright X-ray emission for nearly ten minutes.

Neutron stars are extremely dense stellar remnants left behind after massive stars reach the ends of their lives. When two of them merge, they generate gravitational waves, and the light produced can help astronomers determine what survives the collision. Researchers in Professor Eleonora Troja's group concluded that they may have witnessed the formation of a magnetar produced by the merger. The study was published in Science Bulletin.

"However, if the remnant of the collision is a magnetar, it could keep bursting for longer," said Troja, who is a co-corresponding author of the paper. She explained that magnetars are rapidly spinning neutron stars with huge magnetic fields, and that when they damp their magnetic power into the surroundings, they can make an explosion brighter and longer-lasting.

The follow-up work was a race against time. After an alert from the Einstein Probe, the team organized observations with several instruments, including the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope (VLT) and the Very Large Array. Graduate student Niccolò Passaleva led the VLT observations in Chile and responded within minutes. "I was traveling home by train," recalls Passaleva, "and all of a sudden I was rushing against time to commandeer one of the largest telescopes in the world from my laptop."

Using the VLT's X-Shooter instrument, the team split the event's light into its individual components and measured a redshift of z=0.6610. Redshift reveals how far away a source is. According to the researchers, the explosion happened long before our Sun and its planets formed, and its light traveled for more than six billion years before reaching Earth. The team also used the VLT's FORS2 instrument to look for a bright supernova, which would normally be expected if a long-lasting X-ray flash came from the collapse of a massive star.

"This is the longest lasting prompt X-ray flash ever observed from a neutron star merger," said Passaleva.

The researchers had spent several years looking for a firm connection between fast X-ray transients and neutron star mergers, but earlier candidates faded too quickly to provide enough evidence. The study presents strong evidence for that connection, and it raises the possibility that some mysterious cosmic flashes may come from merging neutron stars.
why_it_matters: The study gives astronomers a possible way to find and understand extreme collisions in space. It also shows how quick follow-up observations can capture rare events while they are still bright.

background_read: The Einstein Probe is a satellite launched in January 2024, and the article says it has detected hundreds of bright X-ray flashes from distant galaxies.
The Very Large Telescope (VLT) is operated by the European Southern Observatory and is in Chile.
The study was published in Science Bulletin.
